title: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information
summary: Deobfuscation is the step in which an attacker converts deliberately hidden data back into something usable on the victim system. The initial file, script or registry value is not the real payload; it is a container holding encoded, compressed, encrypted or split content, and the real behaviour only appears once the container is unpacked. Attackers rarely ship a decoder of their own, because the operating system already offers one: the certificate utility can decode a base64 blob hidden inside a certificate file, the copy and type commands can concatenate numbered fragments back into a single binary, and PowerShell, JavaScript or a macro can reverse a custom encoding in memory. The technique is therefore less a specific tool and more a class of behaviour in which a decoding utility touches a suspicious file, or a script writes a second file that it then executes. Two variants matter for detection. In the fully automated variant no prompt appears and the decoded content is written to a temporary path or loaded straight into memory. In the user assisted variant the operator sends a password protected archive and the victim supplies the password, which is why user execution is often the trigger that makes the rest of the chain possible. The defender's discriminator is provenance and sequence rather than the command itself, because the same decoders are used by administrators, installers and backup software every day. What separates abuse is a decoding command whose input came from a mail attachment or download folder, whose output is an executable, script or archive, and whose output is started moments later, often with the decoded file sitting in a temporary directory and disappearing soon afterwards.

beginner.definition: Deobfuscation means turning scrambled data back into its normal form. An attacker hides their harmful file in a scrambled package, then unscrambles it on your computer. The unscrambling is the deobfuscation step.
beginner.whyItMatters: Scrambled files often pass security tools that only look for known bad patterns. The attacker does not need to write a decoder, because normal system tools can do the job. When a helper tool like the certificate utility is used, it looks like ordinary administration work.
howItWorks: The attacker hides the real payload by encoding it, compressing it or splitting it.
The hidden payload is then delivered, often inside an email attachment or a download.
A decoder runs on your machine, either built into the malware or a system utility.
The decoder writes the real file to disk, or rebuilds it in memory.
The attacker then runs the decoded file to carry on with the attack.
In some cases the file is password protected and you must type the password.
beginner.example: Think of a parcel that arrives as a flat pack of planks with no screws. The courier also left a screwdriver in your hallway. You assemble the table yourself and it looks like any other table. On the doorstep, the flat pack looked harmless, and the screwdriver belonged to the house.
takeaways: Decoding is normal behaviour, so watch what is decoded and where it goes next.
A decoder writing an executable to a temporary folder is a strong warning sign.
If a file needs your password to open, that step is part of the attack.

objectives: Explain the difference between obfuscation and deobfuscation in an intrusion.
Describe how built in system utilities can be used to decode hidden content.
Explain why user action may be required before a payload can be decoded.
Identify process creation logs and file writes that show a decoding step.
Explain why the same tools appear in legitimate administrative work.
